title: Reinforcement learning: learning to act from rewards

items.context:
The tank agent uses a discount factor γ = 0.95, one decision every 0.5 time units. Roughly
how far ahead does it look?
items.why:
A reward k steps away counts γ^k as much as one now, so the effective horizon is roughly
1/(1 − γ) = 20 steps. That is four times as long as the tank takes to fill from 2 to 5 at
full inflow, long enough to see the overshoot an early valve opening causes.
items.true: About 20 steps, or 10 time units
false: One step, because Q-learning only ever looks at the next state
The whole 100-step episode, equally weighted at every step
About 95 steps, one for each hundredth of the discount

items.context: If you knew the Q-function of the best policy, Q*(s, a), how would you act?
items.why:
Q*(s, a) is the expected return from taking a in s and then acting optimally. With it in hand,
acting well is a lookup: the best action is the one with the largest value.
items.true: In each state, take the action with the largest Q*(s, a)
false: Sample actions in proportion to their Q-values in each state
Take the action with the largest immediate reward in each state
Keep exploring at random one time in five, forever

items.context:
A team's learned reactor controller behaves strangely. Its state is the reactor temperature
alone, and the catalyst has been deactivating for a week. What is the first thing to check?
items.why:
The Markov property is a modelling choice. Temperature alone does not determine the next
temperature when the catalyst is changing, so the state has to include the deactivation, or
something that tracks it.
items.true: Whether the state leaves out something the dynamics depend on
false: The learning rate, because a deactivating catalyst needs a larger α
The discount factor, which should be 1 for a continuous process
Whether the reward is scaled to between 0 and 1

items.context:
A corridor of eight cells pays +1 only at the right end. With one-step Q-learning updates,
how does that reward reach the first cell?
items.why:
Each update reads the next cell's estimate through the max term, which is bootstrapping. So
the news travels back one cell per episode. Monte Carlo, which waits for the whole return,
fills the corridor in one episode at the price of variance.
items.true: One cell further back per episode, discounted each time
false: All at once, after the first episode that reaches the end
Never, because cells far from the reward are never updated
Only if the reward is moved to the start of the corridor

items.context:
A run with catalyst B gives a yield of 70%. What kind of feedback is that, and what does it
leave out?
items.why:
Instructive feedback names the right answer whatever the learner did; every label in L9 and
L10 is one. Evaluative feedback scores the choice made and nothing else, which is what forces
a reinforcement learner to explore.
items.true: Evaluative: it scores B and says nothing about the catalysts not tried
false: Instructive: it names the right catalyst for this reaction
Instructive: it is a labelled data point like any regression target
Evaluative: it ranks every catalyst relative to B at once

items.context:
Bayesian optimization (L15) and reinforcement learning both learn from scores. What does
reinforcement learning have that Bayesian optimization does not?
items.why:
Running a reaction at 80 °C today does not change what 90 °C will give tomorrow, so each
experiment is a fresh decision. In reinforcement learning the action changes the state, and
through it every later reward.
items.true: Actions that change the state the learner faces next
false: A surrogate model linking the choices that were tried
Noise in the measured outcome of each choice it makes
An acquisition function trading exploration against exploitation

items.context:
"Reinforcement learning from human feedback lets a person grade every output the model
writes." What did InstructGPT actually optimize with PPO?
items.why:
The paper trains a reward model on labelers' comparisons and then uses it as the reward for
PPO. The environment is a learned stand-in for a person's judgement, so it can be gamed like
any other reward.
items.true: A reward model trained to predict which output labelers would prefer
false: Labelers' scores, collected live for every output during training
The next-token loss on a larger set of human-written answers
The number of tokens in each answer, as a proxy for helpfulness

items.context: In the Q-learning update, what is the bracket r + γ max Q(s', a') − Q(s, a)?
items.why:
The temporal-difference error compares the one-step target with the current estimate, and
the learning rate α sets how far each sample moves the entry toward it.
items.true: The TD error: what the step suggests minus what the table says
false: The reward the agent expects at the end of the episode
The probability of choosing a random action at this step
The gradient of the policy with respect to the network weights

items.context: Why does the tank agent pick a random inflow one time in five (ε-greedy, ε = 0.2)?
items.why:
An entry for an action that is never taken never moves. Watkins and Dayan's convergence proof
requires all actions to be sampled repeatedly in all states, so exploration is a mathematical
requirement as well as a practical one.
items.true: The table only learns about actions that get tried
false: To keep the valve from wearing out in one position
To add noise that makes the learned policy robust to sensors
Because the PID baseline also uses random perturbations

items.context:
From one start (h = 2), the trained agent beats a PID loop with hand-picked gains. Then the
PID is tuned, and both are tested from eight starting levels with ten training seeds. What
happens?
items.why:
Over eight starts the agent's error was 1.40 ± 1.31 against 0.19 for the tuned PID. Half the
seeds matched the tuned PID; the other half failed from at least one start they rarely saw in
training.
items.true: The tuned PID wins, by about a factor of seven on average
false: The agent still wins, since it learned from the tank itself
They tie, because both settle exactly on the setpoint
The comparison cannot be made, since the agent uses five inflows

items.context:
The tank's outflow is k√h with k = 0.5, and the agent chooses inflow from {0, 0.5, 1, 1.5,
2}. Why does it switch back and forth near the setpoint of 5?
items.why:
At steady state F = k√h, so the five inflows hold levels 0, 1, 4, 9 and 16. No policy over
this action set can hold 5; the best it can do is alternate, which is what the saw-tooth is.
items.true: No allowed inflow holds h = 5; that needs F = 1.118
false: Its learning rate is too high, so the table never settles
The reward penalizes standing still at any single level
The 20 level bins are too coarse to see the setpoint at all

items.context:
To fix the switching, the action set grows from five inflows to nine, with the same 1,000
training episodes. What happened to the error over eight starts?
items.why:
A bigger table needs more experience to fill, and the budget did not change. Discretization
has a cost on each side, and a continuous action is one reason deep RL methods exist.
items.true: It was 0.99 ± 0.94: 180 entries need more data than 100
false: It fell to match the tuned PID, since 1.0 and 1.25 bracket 1.118 closely
It was unchanged, because the level bins limit accuracy
It fell to zero, because one of the nine inflows holds h = 5

items.context:
The tank's reward becomes −|h(t+1) − h(t)|, "keep the level steady". Where does the trained
agent leave the level?
items.why:
The reward only penalizes movement, so the agent parks the tank at the nearest
constant-inflow steady state and leaves it there. The level is steady, the setpoint was never
in the reward, and the error from 5 is 9.69. This is specification gaming.
items.true: At 1, 4 or 9: a level one constant inflow holds
false: At the setpoint, 5, where a good controller keeps it
Empty, at 0, from every starting level it is given
Wherever it started, by closing the inflow completely

items.context:
"DeepMind used reinforcement learning to cut Google's data-centre cooling energy by 40%."
What do the sources say?
items.why:
The 2016 blog reports "up to 40 percent" from neural-network predictions and never uses the
words. Lazic et al. (2018) learned a linear model from three hours of exploration and used MPC,
with "the potential to save about 9%".
items.true: The blog never says RL; the paper is a linear model with MPC, about 9%
false: The 2018 paper confirms a 40% saving from a deep RL agent
The 40% came from replacing PID loops with a tuned PID controller
The saving was measured on a simulator and never deployed

items.context:
A unit has several interacting variables and constraints, and you can fit a dynamic model of
it. Which tool is usually right?
items.why:
MPC fits a model, optimizes the actions over a horizon, applies the first and repeats. With
a usable model it needs far fewer samples than model-free RL; Recht found policy gradient
needed thousands of times as many samples as simple nominal control on LQR.
items.true: Model predictive control
false: Reinforcement learning, because the variables interact
Bayesian optimization, one variable at a time, in sequence
A generative model of past operating data

items.context:
On the three-level tank, the operator opens at low and shuts otherwise. Starting at low the
tank goes low, ok, low, ok and so on, earning 0.9, 0, 0.9, 0 and so on. With rewards k steps
ahead counted as 0.9^k times their size, what is the value of starting at low?
items.why:
The rewards repeat every two steps, and each repeat counts 0.9^2 = 0.81 times the one before,
so the total is 0.9 (1 + 0.81 + 0.81^2 + ...) = 0.9 / 0.19 = 4.737. Dividing by 1 - 0.9
would count a reward of 0.9 on every step, but every second step earns nothing.
false: 0.9, the reward of the first step
Infinite, since the cycle never ends

items.context:
Value iteration updates every entry of Q with R + γ P_a V. Q-learning uses no matrices at
all. What exactly does it replace?
items.why:
Q-learning moves one entry a fraction α toward r + γ max Q(s′, ·) for the observed s′. Over
many visits s′ lands in each column of row s of P_a in proportion to its probability, so the
average update is the value-iteration update: a sample update instead of an expected one.
items.true: The expectation P_a V, with the value of the one next state actually observed
false: The reward matrix R, with a learned reward model
The max over actions, with an average over actions
The discount γ, with the learning rate α

items.context:
Half the Q-learning seeds on the 20-bin tank fail badly from some start. Solving the tank's
own 20 × 20 transition matrices exactly, with the same five inflows and the same bins, gives
a policy that scores 0.187 over the eight starts, about the tuned PID's 0.19. What does that
say about the failing seeds?
items.why:
The exact solution uses the same representation and matches PID, so nothing about the
table forced the loss. The bad seeds picked, in a rarely visited bin, an inflow that holds
the level inside that bin (0.5 in bin 1, 1.5 in bin 17), a diagonal 1 in P_a, so the tank
parks there.
items.true: The table and the five inflows were enough; the failures came from learning
false: Five inflows cannot hold the setpoint, so every table policy must lose to PID
The bins are not Markov, so no table can be trusted on this tank
The failing seeds needed a larger discount factor

items.context:
On the three-level tank (levels ordered low, ok, high), the valve sometimes sticks, so row
low of the matrix for opening is [0.2, 0.8, 0]. What does the 0.8 mean?
items.why:
The row is where the tank is (low), the column is where it ends up (ok), and the entry is the
chance of that move under this action. Scores live in a separate table, R, and the matrix
says nothing about how often the tank is anywhere.
items.true: Opening from low reaches ok four times in five
false: Opening from low earns a score of 0.8
The tank is at ok 80% of the time
Opening from ok returns to low four times in five

items.context:
The three-level tank's Q table starts at zero, with alpha = 0.5 and gamma = 0.9. After one
update Q(low, open) = 0.45. Now the program, at ok, shuts and lands at low with a score of
0. What does Q(ok, shut) become?
items.why:
The target is the score plus 0.9 times the best entry in the row where the move landed, and
the best entry in row low is 0.45, so the target is 0.405. With alpha = 0.5 the entry moves
halfway from 0 to 0.405, to 0.2025. The score of 0 does not make the target 0, because
landing at low is worth something when you can open from there.
items.true: About 0.20, half of the target 0 + 0.9 x 0.45
false: 0, because the score was 0
0.405, the target itself
0.45, copied from Q(low, open)
